name: Priya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group without ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. I keep this confidential. What was your day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was checking a small care agency's payroll and tax return, and one night's overtime had been put on the wrong worker. I'm 43, a team lead at West Pier Accounts, with a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification; people bring me the hard payslip questions because I'm one of the best at this desk. I enjoy straightening out a wage before someone is underpaid, and I dread telling a client I need another day because a timesheet arrived late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household like, and do you work with AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Malik is a cook on late shifts, and our children are eight and thirteen. We have a mortgage, my pay is low for a senior accountant, less than a month of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby. I do not use AI tools; I check the timesheet and payslip myself, and I am slow to trust a new system. I tend to look for the practical answer rather than take a side in every argument about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the carers a quick timesheet sort might help, but a person still has to see who worked the late shift. I wouldn't promise software can settle a pay dispute by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead job probably holds, yet my salary is low for it and we have almost no buffer after the mortgage. One quiet week for Malik in the kitchen could make the next payment tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking care payroll from timesheets to payslips and ask the partners for a pay review based on the cases I resolve. Starting this month we'd stop buying Friday takeaway and put forty each month into a separate mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about bills, though not because of this small AI change. A senior title cannot cover a payment on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring to the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care worker whose night hours were put against the wrong name. I found it by asking for the signed rota, not by looking at a glossy report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pay review solve the buffer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a raise is agreed in writing, and I would not spend it before that. The forty comes from a real cut in takeaway spending.

I would ask for a **human checker** before payslips go out.
think: My **lead role** likely holds, but pay is low for it.
A **thin mortgage buffer** makes Malik’s quiet weeks matter.
do: Keep checking **timesheets and payslips** under current review.
Save **forty monthly** by dropping Friday takeaway.
Request a **written pay review** based on resolved cases.
feel: She feels **anxious** because bills strain a thin cushion.
S0.quote: A senior title cannot cover a payment on its own.
fieldNote: Her strongest work is **wage dispute checking**, yet her senior salary remains low.
She expects no quick AI shock but will not count a **raise before writing** it into household cash.

steps.text: Keep checking care-worker timesheets against payslips
Save forty monthly by dropping Friday takeaway
Request written pay review using resolved wage disputes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners which payroll checks the software takes and what paid work is left for my team. If they want a new system, they should demonstrate it with a person responsible for the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can check wages and write client replies, which is a lot of my day. I think the firm may cut a junior post first, but my own hours could shrink if clients stop paying for human review; our savings won't carry a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staffing plan and watch a paid demonstration on old care files with the senior if the firm requires it. In the first year of steady change, if my paid week falls below four days, I'd apply for posted payroll jobs at the one other accounting firm on the bus line while keeping West Pier hours until a written wage and start date are agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the chance my own pay shrinks. I do not want to learn an untested tool on a worker's live wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the current files by hand and ask the partners to put the hours plan in writing. I might read the tool's paper guide, but I would not run client data through it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other firm posts nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on paid West Pier work and ask for a wage discussion there. A job that has not been advertised cannot pay this mortgage.

I would require a **responsible human** on machine wages.
think: My **own hours** could shrink if clients stop paying for review.
Our **thin reserve** cannot carry an uncertain search.

Keep hand checks and **paid hours** if the demonstration is unpaid; request a written hours plan.
Apply for **posted bus-line payroll** work below four paid days, keeping West Pier hours until written terms.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a realistic cut to her own pay.

fieldNote: She will watch a **paid required demonstration** but refuses unsupervised use on live wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the care agencies that full AGI in 2028 can do the account and tax thinking, so someone must still answer for a wrong wage. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, too late to shield my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect West Pier to cut paid payroll review sharply and could lose my lead job, even with my skill. Malik's hands-on cooking may face robots later, so our mortgage could meet two losses with less than one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd stop the planned new sofa and add its seventy monthly instalment to our mortgage buffer. In the first year after 2028, if my role ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried payroll-control posts at local care agencies and ask my sister to cover school pickup only if a real written paid offer names the actual start time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. There are few local accounting posts and the lender needs money, not a certificate of skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister manage pickup for long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for one school term, and I would arrange it after a real written paid offer names the actual start time. I would reject unpaid work; I would not use her help to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care agencies have no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep any paid West Pier account checks and use the buffer for mortgage bills. I won't assume standing beside a paper file keeps a thinking job safe from AGI.

say: I would ask for a **named wage reviewer** after AGI.
I would separate **2028 desk risk** from later robots.
think: My **lead payroll role** could disappear when AGI takes wage and tax thinking work in 2028.
Malik’s **cooking wage** may face robots around 2031.
do: Save **seventy monthly** by delaying the sofa.
Apply for **advertised care payroll** work after 2028 job loss.

feel: She feels **alarmed** about a likely pay loss and thin reserve.

fieldNote: Her high skill does not remove **2028 desk exposure** or the later robot risk to Malik’s cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a firm time to explain what it will pay humans to check and a family time to save. I would want a staffing answer, not a list of fashionable roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 the children will still need us, and the mortgage will not be gone. AGI could do the payroll reasoning I am good at, while Malik's hands-on kitchen work may face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add fifty a month from pay to our mortgage buffer and ask the partners for written pay and staffing plans by next tax season. In the first year after 2031, if West Pier cuts my paid role, I'd apply for posted salaried payroll supervisor jobs at nearby care agencies, keeping any funded firm hours until a written wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because five years helps the bank account but doesn't make a posted job. I still have less than a month saved today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a new course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a care payroll course only if a care agency posts a paid supervisor role requiring it and funds the fee and study time. I would not pay for a course just to escape a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if there is no course or vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the current payroll and saving fifty a month from our wages. I'd ask the partners for real hours instead of taking unpaid training leave.

I would require **paid work** behind any new role.

My **payroll reasoning** remains exposed to AGI.
do: Save **fifty monthly** into the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives families time to reduce a loan and employers time to state which payroll review still earns a wage. I would not say a person is safe just because they look at paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would still need income, though the children might be older and the loan smaller. AGI reaches the thinking in my payroll desk then; robots around 2039 could affect Malik's cooking later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay an extra one hundred monthly against the mortgage while both wages hold and keep checking current care returns. In the first year after 2036, if West Pier cuts my lead salary, I'd apply for posted salaried payroll posts nearby and retain any available paid West Pier hours until a written loan-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money today, even with a decade to plan. A future smaller loan does not make this month's mortgage payment easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Malik loses shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra principal payment and hold that cash for food and bills. I would not buy a training package while the household pay is down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if you paid the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we have less than a month saved today and still have children to support. I would rather keep earning and let any future savings grow from real wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could go before we have one mortgage payment saved. A written staffing answer and a posted salaried care-payroll job would help. My title is senior; our savings are not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who calls the worker when a machine puts a night shift on the wrong payslip. A wage mistake is a missing dinner in somebody's house, not just a number to correct.

headlineQuote: A wage mistake is a missing dinner in somebody's house, not just a number to correct.
portrait: Priya, **43**, leads care payroll checks at West Pier with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
She is **highly skilled** but paid below her level, with under a month saved and few nearby accounting posts.
She **never uses AI**, while Malik’s cooking wage supports their two school-age children and mortgage.
She fears **2028 lead-pay loss** and uses written staffing plans, cash saving and posted salaried work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before one mortgage payment is saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing answer** and posted salaried care-payroll job would help.
